mainTopic: The משנה of those executed by חנק, and the rules for one who strikes a parent: a blow alone, a wound, and wounding for healing
overview: The new פרק opens with a משנה listing the sinners whom בית דין executes by חנק. The גמרא starts with one who strikes a parent. It brings a פסוק and the rule that any unspecified death in the תורה is חנק. It then proves that a blow alone is enough, without killing, because when the תורה means killing it adds 'and he dies.' Next it asks why the striker is liable only for a wound. It first compares striking a person to striking an animal. After רב ירמיה's challenge, it learns the wound rule from the extra word נפש instead. The comparison is still needed, either for the teaching of the school of חזקיה or to teach that striking for healing is exempt, so a son may let blood for his father. The גמרא then discusses why רב and מר בריה דרבינא would not let their sons treat them, and compares this to removing a thorn on שבת. The discussion of רבי שמעון's view on a destructive wound continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The list of those executed by strangulation
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists eight kinds of sinners who receive the death penalty of חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the people executed by strangulation: one who strikes his father or mother, one who kidnaps a Jew, a זקן ממרא who rebels against the court's ruling, a false prophet, one who prophesies in the name of עבודה זרה, a man who has relations with a married woman, the עדים זוממין who falsely accused a כהן's daughter, and the man who actually had relations with her.
steps.whatsHappening: The new פרק opens with a משנה that simply lists everyone whom בית דין executes by חנק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the last of the four court deaths to get its own list, after סקילה, שריפה and הרג. Notice the last case: a כהן's daughter who sins is burned, but the false witnesses against her and the man involved get חנק, not burning.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who are executed by strangulation
A kidnapper (literally, one who steals a person)
A rebellious elder, a scholar who rules against the high court
A false prophet
Conspiring witnesses, false witnesses who are caught

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the witnesses against a כהן's daughter get the same death she would have gotten. She gets burning; they and her partner get חנק.

phrases.english: MISHNA: These are the ones who are strangled:
One who strikes his father or his mother,
and one who kidnaps a Jewish person,

phrases.aramaic: וְזָקֵן מַמְרֵא עַל פִּי בֵּית דִּין,
phrases.english: and a rebellious elder against the ruling of the court,
and a false prophet,
and one who prophesies in the name of idol worship,
and one who has relations with a married woman,
and the conspiring witnesses against a priest's daughter, and her partner.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eight categories of sinners are executed by חנק, including one who strikes a parent and the עדים זוממין of a כהן's daughter.

steps.title: What is the source for striking a parent?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that one who strikes a parent is executed by חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who strikes his father or mother: from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with the first case in the משנה and asks for its source in the תורה. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants a פסוק for two things: that striking a parent is a capital crime, and that the death is specifically חנק.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?
One who strikes

phrases.english: GEMARA: One who strikes his father or his mother —
from where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the first case listed in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source that striking a parent is punished by חנק.

steps.title: The verse plus the rule for unspecified death
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says the striker 'shall be put to death,' and any death the תורה gives without naming a method is חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'One who strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.' And every death mentioned in the תורה without details is only strangulation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק that makes striking a parent a capital crime. It then adds a general rule that tells us which death is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'מות יומת' but doesn't name the method. The rule 'כל מיתה האמורה בתורה סתם אינה אלא חנק' fills in the gap: when no method is named, it is חנק.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall surely be put to death
Without details, unspecified
Strangulation

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that an unspecified death means חנק is used for many of the cases in this פרק.

phrases.english: As it is written: "One who strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death,"
and every death stated in the Torah without specifying how —
is nothing other than strangulation.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב וּמַכֵּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'ומכה אביו ואמו מות יומת' together with the rule that an unspecified death is חנק.

steps.title: Maybe he must actually kill the parent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that perhaps the death penalty applies only if he actually kills his parent, not for a mere blow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that he is only executed if he kills him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how far the פסוק reaches: maybe 'strikes' here means a deadly blow that kills the parent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'מכה' can sometimes mean a killing blow. If so, the crime in the פסוק would be killing a parent, not just hitting one.

keyTerms.meaning: Say, maybe (introduces a suggested reading)
Only once he kills him

phrases.english: Say: he is not executed until he kills him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the scope of the פסוק cited in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that striking alone, without killing, brings the death penalty.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'מכה' might mean a fatal blow, so the פסוק may only cover killing a parent.

steps.title: Killing a parent can't be punished less than killing a stranger
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion: a murderer of anyone gets the sword, so it makes no sense that killing a parent gets the lighter death of חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think so? If he kills anyone else, he gets the sword, but if he kills his father, only strangulation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: if the פסוק were about killing a parent, the parent-killer would get a lighter death than an ordinary murderer, which is unreasonable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A regular murderer is killed by סייף. If the פסוק meant killing a parent, the punishment would be חנק, which this answer treats as a lighter death. Since killing a parent can't be less serious than killing a stranger, the פסוק must be about a blow that does not kill.

keyTerms.meaning: Would it enter your mind? (rejects an idea as unreasonable)
The sword, execution by beheading

phrases.english: Does it enter your mind?
If he kills some other person, he dies by the sword,
but if he kills his father, by strangulation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical argument from relative severity of punishments
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק applies only when the son kills the parent.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק must be about a blow that does not kill, since killing a parent can't be punished more lightly than killing a stranger.

steps.title: The answer fails if strangulation is the harsher death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the last answer only works if חנק is lighter than the sword; for the view that חנק is harsher, the question comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says strangulation is lighter. But for the one who says strangulation is harsher, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own answer. That answer depends on one side of a known argument about which death is more severe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חנק is harsher than סייף, then giving a parent-killer חנק would be a stricter punishment, which makes perfect sense. So by that view, the פסוק could still be about killing a parent, and the question from step 4 is open again.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (for one view)
Lighter, more lenient
Harsher, more severe
What is there to say?

steps.confusionAlert: The question isn't against the משנה's ruling. It only says the answer of step 5 doesn't work by every view.

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says strangulation is lighter,
phrases.notes: This is the argument over which of the four deaths is lightest: the רבנן say חנק, while רבי שמעון says the sword is lighter.

phrases.english: but according to the one who says strangulation is harsher,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5 by showing it depends on one side of a dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument in step 5 that killing a parent can't get חנק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If חנק is harsher than סייף, then giving it to a parent-killer is a fitting stricter punishment, so the פסוק could still mean killing a parent.

steps.title: Plain 'striking' in the Torah means a blow, not a killing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new proof. When the תורה means a killing, it adds 'and he dies.' So a plain 'striking' means only a blow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn it from what is written: 'One who strikes a man and he dies shall be put to death,' and also: 'Or if in hatred he struck him with his hand and he died.' Learn from this: anywhere the תורה just says 'striking,' it does not mean death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6 in a new way. It shows that 'one who strikes his father or mother' means a blow, not a killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5's answer only worked if חנק is lighter than the sword, so the גמרא drops it. The new proof comes from wording. In murder cases the תורה adds 'and he dies' (ומת), so when the פסוק about a parent says only 'strikes,' with no 'and he dies,' it means a blow alone. This answer works no matter which death is harsher.

keyTerms.meaning: From what is written. It introduces a proof from a פסוק.
Plain striking, with no mention of death.
Learn from it. It introduces the lesson drawn from the source.
Death, meaning the blow caused the person to die.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think 'strikes' here means 'kills.' The whole point is the opposite: because the murder פסוקים had to add 'and he dies,' plain 'strikes' means only hitting.

phrases.english: Rather, from that which is written:
'One who strikes a man and he dies shall be put to death,'
and it is written: 'Or if in hatred he struck him with his hand and he died,'
learn from this:
anywhere there is plain 'striking' –
it is not talking about death.
phrases.notes: So 'one who strikes his father or mother' (שמות 21:15) means a blow alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised in step 6 with a new proof that does not depend on which death is harsher.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New proof from the wording of the פסוקים, replacing the earlier logical argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the parent-striker is executed only if he actually kills the parent.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תורה writes 'and he dies' when it means killing. Plain 'strikes' means a blow alone, so the parent-striker is executed even without killing.

steps.title: Why the Torah needs two separate murder verses
steps.stepSummary: A side note: both murder פסוקים, 'one who strikes a man' and 'anyone who strikes a soul,' are needed. Each one alone could be misunderstood.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה needed to write 'one who strikes a man' and also 'anyone who strikes a soul.' With only 'a man,' I would think only an adult counts and not a child. With only 'a soul,' I would think even a baby who cannot live, or an eight-month baby, counts. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא just quoted the murder פסוקים, it pauses to explain why the תורה wrote more than one. This is a side point, not part of the main argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A man' alone suggests only an adult who keeps מצוות, so the second פסוק adds that killing a child also counts. 'A soul' alone could include a baby that cannot survive (a נפל or a בן שמונה), so the word 'man' limits it to a viable person. Each פסוק fixes the mistake the other could cause.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed.
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה.
I would have said, a mistaken first thought.
Babies born unable to survive.
A baby born in the eighth month, treated in the times of the גמרא as unable to survive.
They are both needed.

phrases.english: And it was necessary to write 'one who strikes a man,'
and it was necessary to write 'anyone who strikes a soul.'
For if the Merciful One had written only 'one who strikes a man and he dies,'
I would have said:
a man who is obligated in מצוות – yes,
a child – no.
So the Merciful One wrote 'anyone who strikes a soul.'
And if the Merciful One had written only 'anyone who strikes a soul,'
I would have said:
even babies who cannot survive, even an eight-month baby.
So both are needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side note explaining why the murder פסוקים quoted in step 7 are not repetitive.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both murder פסוקים are needed. One includes killing a child, and the other leaves out a baby who cannot survive.

steps.title: Why is a wound required for striking a parent?
steps.stepSummary: If a plain blow is enough, why does the משנה say the striker is liable only if he makes a wound?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say he is liable even if he did not make a wound! Why then did we learn: one who strikes his father or mother is not liable unless he makes a wound on them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new proof. If any blow counts, why does the משנה require a wound?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 showed that the parent-striker is executed for a blow, not a killing. But nothing in that proof says the blow must draw blood. The משנה (85b) clearly requires a חבורה, so the גמרא asks where that requirement comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: But let me say. It introduces a challenging suggestion.
A wound that draws blood.
Why then did we learn? It points to a משנה that contradicts the suggestion.

phrases.english: But say:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא עָבֵיד בֵּיהּ חַבּוּרָה?
phrases.english: even though he did not make a wound on him?
Why then did we learn:
one who strikes his father or his mother

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה בָּהֶן חַבּוּרָה!
phrases.english: is not liable unless he makes a wound on them!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא עָבֵיד בֵּיהּ חַבּוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the main line after the side note and challenges the result of step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion of step 7 that a plain blow to a parent brings the death penalty.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The proof from the פסוקים includes any blow, but the משנה requires a wound. Where does that requirement come from?

steps.title: Striking a person is compared to striking an animal
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק puts striking a person next to striking an animal. Striking an animal requires a wound, so striking a person does too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'One who strikes an animal… and one who strikes a person.' Just as one who strikes an animal is liable only if he makes a wound, since 'soul' is written about it, so too one who strikes a person is liable only if he makes a wound.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It learns the wound requirement by comparing striking a person to striking an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק places the two cases side by side, so they share the same rule. About an animal the תורה says 'strikes the soul (נפש),' and נפש is linked to blood, so a wound that draws blood is needed. The same rule carries over to striking a person, which explains the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: One who strikes an animal.
Soul. Here it hints at blood, so a wound is needed.
Just as… so too. It sets up a comparison between two cases.

steps.whatToRemember: One who strikes a parent gets חנק for a blow alone, because plain 'striking' in the תורה is not killing. But he is liable only if he draws blood (חבורה). This step learns that from the comparison to an animal, but רב ירמיה challenges that source in step 11, and step 12 gives a new one.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule of the משנה: hitting a parent is a capital crime only when the blow makes a wound.

phrases.english: The פסוק says:
'One who strikes a person and one who strikes an animal.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:21. The two cases appear in the same פסוק.

phrases.english: Just as one who strikes an animal –
is not liable until he makes a wound on it,
since 'soul' is written about it,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:18 says 'one who strikes the soul of an animal.' 'Soul' points to blood, so a wound is needed.

phrases.english: so too one who strikes a person –
is not liable until he makes a wound.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by giving a source for the wound requirement in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparison of two cases placed together in one פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any blow to a parent, even without a wound, brings the death penalty.
steps.terutzMaskana: Striking a person is like striking an animal. Since 'soul' points to blood, liability requires a wound.

steps.title: Damaging an animal without a wound still makes you pay
steps.stepSummary: רב ירמיה challenges the comparison to an animal. Someone who hurts an animal by loading it with stones pays even though there is no wound.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ירמיה objected: If so, if someone weakened an animal by loading stones on it, would he also not be liable? Of course he is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ירמיה attacks the answer from Step 10. That answer said striking an animal needs a wound, so striking a parent needs a wound too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The premise of Step 10 is false. If you hurt someone's animal in any way, even by overloading it with stones and causing no bleeding, you must pay. So the animal case cannot teach that a wound is required.

keyTerms.meaning: He objected to it (a strong challenge)
But if that is so (introduces a problem with what was just said)
He weakened it (hurt the animal without a wound)

phrases.english: Rav Yirmeya objected to it:
But if that is so,
if he weakened it with stones,
phrases.notes: He loaded the animal with heavy stones and hurt it, but never made it bleed.

phrases.english: would he also not be liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב יִרְמְיָה: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the comparison to an animal brought in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 10 that striking an animal is liable only with a wound.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who weakens an animal with stones, with no wound, still pays. So the animal case does not require a wound and cannot teach that rule for a parent.

steps.title: The word 'נפש' is moved over to a person
steps.stepSummary: Since the word נפש is not needed for an animal, it is applied to a person. This teaches that striking a parent needs a wound.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: if the word 'נפש' is not needed for the animal, since even weakening it with stones makes one liable, apply it to a person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees with רב ירמיה and gives a new source for the wound rule, using the method of אם אינו ענין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'one who strikes the נפש of an animal,' and נפש hints at a real wound. For an animal this hint does nothing, because any damage makes one pay. So the hint is applied to striking a person, meaning a parent, who is liable only for a wound.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is not needed for its own topic (then apply it to another topic)
Apply it to the other matter
Soul, life; here it hints at a real wound

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, אִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לְנֶפֶשׁ בְּהֵמָה –
phrases.english: Rather, if it is not relevant to the soul of an animal,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:18. The word נפש appears in 'one who strikes the נפש of an animal.'

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָא אִי נָמֵי הִכְחִישָׁהּ בַּאֲבָנִים חַיָּיב –
phrases.english: since even if he weakened it with stones he is liable,
apply it to the matter of the soul of a person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לְנֶפֶשׁ בְּהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts רב ירמיה's objection and replaces the comparison with a new derivation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wound rule came from comparing a person to an animal.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wound rule comes from the word נפש, which is not needed for an animal and so applies to a person.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule that one who strikes a parent is liable only with a wound comes from the extra word נפש, not from the comparison to an animal.

steps.title: Then why compare a person to an animal at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the wound rule comes from אם אינו ענין, the comparison between a person and an animal seems to teach nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, why do I need the comparison?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the comparison between striking a person and striking an animal is for. Our wound rule now comes from somewhere else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה placed the two strikings next to each other, and that placement should teach something. Once it no longer teaches the wound rule, its purpose must be found.

keyTerms.meaning: A comparison made because the תורה places two things side by side
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: But then, why do I need the comparison?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 12: the comparison now seems to have no job.
steps.kashyaTarget: The purpose of the comparison of person to animal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every comparison in the תורה must teach something. If the wound rule comes from נפש, the comparison is left without a purpose.

steps.title: The comparison teaches the school of חזקיה's rule
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is needed for the teaching of the school of חזקיה about accidental and intentional striking.
steps.simpleTranslation: For that which was taught in the school of חזקיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the comparison teaches the well-known rule from the school of חזקיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That teaching says: just as with striking an animal there is no difference between accidental and intentional, so with striking a person there is no difference. Here the result is that one is exempt from paying money in both cases. So the comparison still has a job.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught (in a ברייתא)
Of the school (study house) of חזקיה

phrases.english: For that which was taught in the school of Chizkiya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13 by giving the comparison a different purpose.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the source to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The comparison has no purpose anymore.
steps.terutzMaskana: The comparison teaches the rule of the school of חזקיה.

steps.title: What about those who reject the school of חזקיה?
steps.stepSummary: The answer works only for those who accept the school of חזקיה. For those who do not, the comparison is again without a purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for one who holds like the תנא of the school of חזקיה. But for one who does not hold like him, why do I need the comparison?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. Not everyone accepts the teaching of the school of חזקיה, so the question comes back for those who don't.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 14 depends on one opinion. For the view that rejects that teaching, the comparison still needs a purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (for one view, but not another)
For the one who holds of it
For the one who does not hold of it

phrases.english: This works out well for the one who holds
like the תנא of the school of Chizkiya,
but for the one who does not hold
like the תנא of the school of Chizkiya,
why do I need the comparison?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאִית לֵיהּ תַּנָּא דְּבֵי חִזְקִיָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that Step 14's answer only works for one opinion.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The school of חזקיה's teaching is disputed. For those who reject it, the comparison still has no purpose.

steps.title: Striking to heal is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The comparison teaches that striking a person for healing is exempt, just like striking an animal for healing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as one who strikes an animal for healing is exempt, so too one who strikes a person for healing is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the comparison a purpose that works even for those who reject the school of חזקיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Treating an animal medically, even when it hurts the animal, does not make one pay. The comparison carries this over to people: striking a person to heal him is exempt. This closes the question of why the comparison is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: For healing, for medical purposes
Exempt, not liable
Just as ... so too (the form of a comparison)

steps.whatToRemember: The wound rule comes from the extra word נפש. The comparison of person to animal teaches either the school of חזקיה's rule or that striking for healing is exempt.

phrases.english: Just as one who strikes an animal for healing is exempt,
so too one who strikes a person for healing is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 15 with a purpose for the comparison that does not depend on the school of חזקיה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the source to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the school of חזקיה, the comparison has no purpose.
steps.terutzMaskana: The comparison teaches that striking a person for healing is exempt, just as with an animal.

steps.title: The question: may a son let blood for his father?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows why the person–animal comparison is needed. There was a real question whether a son may let blood for his father.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the Sages asked: may a son let blood for his father?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the last answer (step 16) by pointing to a real question that was asked. This sets up the two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bloodletting makes a wound, and wounding a parent is a capital crime. So the question is whether a son who does it for healing is still guilty. The comparison from step 16 will be one way to answer this.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the Sages
What is the law?
Bloodletting, a common medical treatment

phrases.english: As a question was raised before them:
phrases.notes: The word 'as' ties this back to step 16. This question is why the person–animal comparison is needed.

phrases.english: A son, what is the law, may he let blood for his father?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical question behind step 16's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a son guilty for wounding his father when he lets blood to heal him?

steps.title: רב מתנא: love your neighbor as yourself
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנא allows it based on the פסוק 'And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנא said: 'And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב מתנא answers the question with a פסוק: a son may let blood for his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as a person wants to be healed himself, he may heal others, even with a wound. Treatment done out of love is not the forbidden 'striking.'

keyTerms.meaning: Love your neighbor as yourself
Neighbor, fellow person

phrases.english: Rav Mattana says:
"And you shall love your neighbor as yourself."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question in step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, he may, based on 'love your neighbor as yourself.'

steps.title: רב דימי בר חיננא: healing a person is like healing an animal
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי בר חיננא allows it from the comparison between striking a person and striking an animal. Healing an animal is exempt, so healing a person is exempt too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי בר חיננא said: striking a person and striking an animal are compared. Just as one who strikes an animal for healing is exempt, so one who strikes a person for healing is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A second answer uses the person–animal comparison. This is the exact use of the comparison that step 16 promised.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה puts striking a person next to striking an animal. Since a wound given to an animal for healing brings no liability, a wound given to a person, even a parent, for healing brings none either.

keyTerms.meaning: One who strikes a person
One who strikes an animal
For healing
Exempt, not liable

steps.whatToRemember: A wound given for healing is not the forbidden 'striking.' This is learned either from 'love your neighbor' or from the person–animal comparison.

phrases.english: Rav Dimi bar Ḥinnana says:
One who strikes a person and one who strikes an animal are compared;
just as one who strikes an animal for healing is exempt,
so too one who strikes a person for healing is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second answer to step 17. It uses the comparison that step 16 said was needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. Striking for healing is exempt, learned from the comparison to an animal.

steps.title: Two אמוראים who would not let their sons treat them
steps.stepSummary: רב would not let his son remove a thorn from him. מר בריה דרבינא would not let his son open his blister. Both worried the son might wound them by mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב did not let his son take out a thorn for him. מר, son of רבינא, did not let his son open a blister for him, in case he wounded him and it became a mistaken sin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how two great אמוראים acted in real life. Even though healing is allowed, they were careful anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is not about planned treatment. It is about a slip: the son might make a wound that wasn't needed, and that would be a sin done by mistake. This sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: A thorn or splinter
A blister
Wounds
A sin done by mistake

phrases.english: Rav did not allow his son
to take out a thorn for him.

phrases.aramaic: מָר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבִינָא לָא שָׁבֵיק לִבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: Mar, son of Ravina, did not allow his son
to open a blister for him,
lest he wound him
and it would be for him a mistaken violation of a prohibition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Even though healing is allowed, these אמוראים were careful because of a possible mistake.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Some were careful not to let a son treat them, because he might wound them by mistake.

steps.title: Why not worry about anyone else too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if that is the worry, it should apply to anyone who treats them, not just a son.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then another person too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason given in step 20. Wounding any Jew is forbidden, so why single out the son?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the problem is a mistaken wound, a stranger could make the same slip. So why did they let others treat them but not their sons?

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Another person, not the son

phrases.english: If so, another person too?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason the אמוראים refused to let their sons treat them.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wounding anyone is forbidden, so the worry should apply to a stranger as well.

steps.title: A son's mistake is far more serious
steps.stepSummary: A stranger's mistake would only be a mistaken לאו. A son's mistake would be a mistaken sin punished by חנק.
steps.simpleTranslation: With another person it is a mistaken negative commandment. With his son it is a mistaken sin punished by strangulation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the level of the sin is different. That is why they were extra careful with a son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wounding any person is a regular לאו. Wounding a parent is a capital crime punished by חנק. The bigger danger of the mistake explains the extra care.

keyTerms.meaning: A negative commandment
Strangulation, a court death penalty

phrases.english: With another, it is a mistaken violation of a negative commandment;
with his son, it is a mistaken violation of a sin punished by strangulation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction by how severe the possible sin is
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A mistaken wound is equally bad whoever does it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A son's mistaken wound is a mistaken capital sin (חנק), so there is more reason to worry.

steps.title: Challenge from removing a thorn on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A משנה allows using a sewing needle to remove a thorn on שבת. Why not worry that he might wound and violate שבת, a sin punished by סקילה?
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned: a hand needle may be used to take out a thorn. Let us worry that he might wound, and it would be a mistaken sin punished by stoning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the whole idea of worrying about a mistaken wound. A משנה does not worry about it even when the sin would be even more severe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wounding on שבת is a סקילה-level sin, worse than חנק. Yet the משנה lets a person remove a thorn without worrying about a slip. So why did the אמוראים worry?

keyTerms.meaning: But what about what we learned in a משנה?
An ordinary hand sewing needle
Let us be concerned
Stoning, the most severe court death penalty

phrases.english: But that which we learned in a mishna:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in שבת 122b, which talks about what may be moved on שבת.

phrases.aramaic: מַחַט שֶׁל יָד לִיטּוֹל בָּהּ אֶת הַקּוֹץ,
phrases.english: a hand needle may be moved to take out a thorn with it;
let us be concerned lest he wound
and it would be a mistaken violation of a sin punished by stoning?
phrases.notes: Making a wound counts as breaking שבת, and breaking שבת is punished by stoning.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָדִתְנַן: מַחַט שֶׁל יָד לִיטּוֹל בָּהּ אֶת הַקּוֹץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the worry about a mistaken wound that was defended in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The concern that the son might wound by mistake (steps 20 and 22).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה does not worry about a mistaken wound even when it would be a סקילה sin, so there should be no worry about a חנק sin either.

steps.title: Wounding while removing a thorn is a destructive act
steps.stepSummary: On שבת, an accidental wound from removing a thorn is מקלקל (destructive), so there is no risk of a serious שבת sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he is being destructive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 23. If he wounds someone while removing a thorn on שבת, that is a destructive act, not a constructive one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rules of שבת are about doing a useful, constructive act. Making a wound by mistake while taking out a thorn only damages the body, so it counts as מקלקל. That is why the משנה does not worry about it, even though a son wounding a parent is still a worry.

keyTerms.meaning: There (pointing back to the case of the thorn on שבת)
One who damages or destroys, doing an act in a destructive way rather than a constructive one

steps.confusionAlert: This does not say wounding is allowed on שבת. It only says that this kind of accidental wound is destructive, so it does not carry the penalty of סקילה.

phrases.english: There, he is being destructive.
phrases.notes: "There" means the thorn on שבת. The wound would only be damage, not a useful act.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 23 by showing that the שבת case is different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: a wound on שבת is מקלקל, while a son wounding a parent is a sin even if it is destructive.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The questioner thought an accidental wound on שבת could bring סקילה, so the משנה should have worried about it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A wound made while removing a thorn is destructive, so it is not a punishable שבת act. There is nothing to worry about.

steps.title: What about the opinion that a destructive act is still liable?
steps.stepSummary: The answer works for the view that מקלקל is exempt, but not for the view that holds him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says a destructive person is exempt. But for the one who says he is liable, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 24. There is an opinion that even a destructive act can make a person liable, so the worry should come back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 depends on the rule that מקלקל is פטור. But there is a dispute about this rule. According to the one who says חייב, an accidental wound on שבת would still be a serious sin, so why does the משנה allow it?

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (for one opinion)
According to the one who says
Exempt, not liable
Liable, deserving punishment
What is there to say? (a way of saying the problem has no answer yet)

phrases.english: This works for the one who says: a destructive person is exempt,
but for the one who says: he is liable,
phrases.notes: He means the opinion that a destructive act on שבת can still make a person liable.

phrases.english: what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 24 by pointing to a different opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the wound is מקלקל and therefore exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That answer only works for one side of a dispute. According to the side that holds a destructive act liable, the risk of סקילה comes back.

steps.title: The opinion that holds a destructive wound liable is רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names who holds that a destructive wound is liable: רבי שמעון. The full answer continues next.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whom did you hear say that one who destroys by wounding is liable? It is רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to answer step 25 by naming who holds the strict opinion: רבי שמעון. This line sets up the next move, which will explain why רבי שמעון would still not worry in the thorn case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of arguing with the strict opinion in general, the גמרא first pins down whose opinion it is. Once we know it is רבי שמעון, we can use his other views to solve the problem. The sentence continues past this point.

keyTerms.meaning: Whom did you hear say this? (a way of naming the source of an opinion)
A wound, an injury that draws blood

steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not finished here. Naming רבי שמעון is only the first half. The גמרא goes on to explain why he too would not worry about the thorn.

phrases.english: Whom did you hear say:
one who destroys by making a wound is liable?
It is רבי שמעון.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins to answer the קשיא of step 25 by naming the author of the strict opinion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Naming the opinion's author, so that his other views can be used to resolve the problem.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The strict opinion seemed to bring back the worry about סקילה in the thorn case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The strict opinion belongs to רבי שמעון. The גמרא is about to show why even he would not hold a person liable here.
